rule_groups.name: Simple Singular vs Plural
rule_groups.explain: A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. Third-person singular verbs usually end in -s.

correct.note: Singular subject 'she' + singular verb 'works' (with -s).

wrong.note: Incorrect: singular subject cannot take a base-form plural verb.

rule_groups.name: Compound Subjects with 'And'
rule_groups.explain: When two subjects are joined by 'and', they usually form a plural subject and need a plural verb.

correct.note: Two distinct subjects joined by 'and' create a plural compound subject.

wrong.note: Incorrect: two subjects joined by 'and' cannot take a singular verb.

rule_groups.name: Compound Subjects with 'Or / Nor'
rule_groups.explain: With 'or' or 'nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it.

correct.text: Neither the students nor the teacher was ready.
correct.note: 'Teacher' is nearer and singular, so the verb is singular.

wrong.text: Neither the students nor the teacher were ready.
wrong.note: Incorrect: proximity rule demands singular 'was' because 'teacher' is closer.

items.before: Either my sister or my brothers
Neither the coach nor the players
Either the dogs or the cat

rule_groups.name: Indefinite Pronouns (Singular)
rule_groups.explain: Pronouns like everyone, someone, anybody, nobody, each, every are grammatically singular and take singular verbs.

correct.note: 'Everyone' is singular in form and takes a singular verb.

wrong.note: Incorrect: indefinite pronouns ending in -one, -body, -thing are singular.

rule_groups.name: Indefinite Pronouns (Plural)
rule_groups.explain: A few indefinite pronouns (both, few, many, several) are always plural and take plural verbs.

correct.note: 'Many' refers to numerous people, so it takes a plural verb.

wrong.note: Incorrect: 'many' is a plural pronoun and cannot take a singular verb.

rule_groups.name: Indefinite Pronouns (Contextual)
rule_groups.explain: Some, all, most, none can be singular or plural depending on the noun they refer to.

correct.note: 'Milk' is uncountable, so 'some' takes a singular verb here.

wrong.note: Incorrect: uncountable nouns require singular verbs regardless of 'some'.

rule_groups.name: Collective Nouns (Singular vs Plural)
rule_groups.explain: Collective nouns (team, family, audience) can take singular or plural verbs depending on whether the group acts as a unit or as individuals.

correct.note: Treating the team as a single unit requires a singular verb.

wrong.note: In American English this is non-standard; the singular is preferred for unified action.

rule_groups.name: Every / Each + Noun
rule_groups.explain: 'Every' and 'each' are singular markers. Even with compound subjects, the verb remains singular.

correct.text: Every boy and girl has a book.
correct.note: 'Every' makes each noun singular, so the compound subject still takes a singular verb.

wrong.text: Every boy and girl have a book.
wrong.note: Incorrect: 'every' forces singular agreement regardless of 'and'.

rule_groups.name: There is / There are
rule_groups.explain: In existential 'there' constructions, the verb agrees with the actual subject that follows it, not with 'there'.

correct.note: The real subject is 'problems' (plural), so the verb must be plural.

wrong.note: Incorrect: the verb must agree with 'problems', not the expletive 'there'.

items.after: two pens and a ruler in the case.

rule_groups.name: Neither / Either + Singular Noun
rule_groups.explain: 'Neither' and 'either' are singular when used with a singular noun. The verb must be singular.

correct.note: 'Neither' + singular noun requires a singular verb.

wrong.note: Incorrect: 'neither' is grammatically singular and demands a singular verb.

rule_groups.name: A Number of / The Number of
rule_groups.explain: 'A number of' means many and takes a plural verb. 'The number of' refers to a figure and takes a singular verb.

correct.note: 'The number' is a singular entity (the figure itself), so it takes a singular verb.

wrong.note: Incorrect: 'the number' is singular; only 'a number of' is plural.

rule_groups.name: None of + Plural Noun
rule_groups.explain: 'None' can take a singular or plural verb, but in formal contexts with countable plurals, the plural is traditional and widely accepted.

correct.note: With countable plural nouns, the plural verb is traditionally preferred.

wrong.note: While 'was' is acceptable in strict singular logic, 'were' is the traditional formal choice for countables.

rule_groups.name: Along with / As well as / Together with
rule_groups.explain: Phrases like 'along with', 'as well as', and 'together with' do not make a subject plural. The verb agrees with the main subject only.

correct.text: The captain, as well as his crew, was rescued.
correct.note: 'As well as his crew' is parenthetical; the main subject 'captain' is singular.

wrong.text: The captain, as well as his crew, were rescued.
wrong.note: Incorrect: intervening phrases do not change the grammatical number of the subject.

items.before: The teacher, along with her students,
The CEO, together with the board members,
My brother, as well as my cousins,
The book, accompanied by a CD,

rule_groups.name: Accompanied by / In addition to / Including
rule_groups.explain: Prepositional phrases such as 'accompanied by', 'in addition to', and 'including' are not part of the grammatical subject.

correct.text: The singer, accompanied by her band, performs tonight.
correct.note: 'Accompanied by her band' is a prepositional modifier; the subject remains singular.

wrong.text: The singer, accompanied by her band, perform tonight.
wrong.note: Incorrect: the verb must agree with the singular subject, not the plural noun in the phrase.

items.before: The president, in addition to his aides,
The house, accompanied by two acres,
The chef, in addition to two sous-chefs,

rule_groups.name: Titles, Names, and Quotations as Subjects
rule_groups.explain: When a title, name, or quotation is the grammatical subject, it is treated as a singular unit even if it contains plural words.

correct.text: 'The Chronicles of Narnia' is a famous series.
correct.note: The title is a singular entity, so the verb is singular despite the plural-sounding name.

wrong.text: 'The Chronicles of Narnia' are a famous series.
wrong.note: Incorrect: a book title is grammatically singular even if it sounds plural.

rule_groups.name: Mathematics, Statistics, Politics, News
rule_groups.explain: Nouns ending in -ics (mathematics, physics, politics) and words like 'news' are usually singular when referring to a field or category.

correct.note: Academic subjects ending in -ics take singular verbs when treated as disciplines.

wrong.note: Incorrect: 'mathematics' as a field of study is grammatically singular.

rule_groups.name: Amount of / Quantity of + Uncountable
rule_groups.explain: 'An amount of' and 'a quantity of' with uncountable nouns take singular verbs. With countable nouns ('a number of'), the verb is plural.

correct.text: A large amount of water was wasted.
correct.note: 'Water' is uncountable, so the verb remains singular.

wrong.text: A large amount of water were wasted.
wrong.note: Incorrect: uncountable nouns paired with 'amount of' require singular verbs.

rule_groups.name: Pair of / Dozen of + Plural Noun
rule_groups.explain: When 'pair of', 'dozen of', or similar expressions are used, the verb usually agrees with 'pair' or 'dozen' (singular), not the plural noun.

correct.text: A pair of shoes is on sale.
correct.note: The head noun is 'pair' (singular), so the verb is singular.

wrong.text: A pair of shoes are on sale.
wrong.note: Incorrect: the grammatical subject is the singular 'pair', not 'shoes'.

rule_groups.name: Relative Clauses: One of + Plural Noun + Who/That
rule_groups.explain: In 'one of those who/that' constructions, the verb in the relative clause is usually plural because its antecedent is the plural noun, not 'one'.

correct.text: She is one of those students who always study hard.
correct.note: The relative clause modifies 'students' (plural), so the verb is plural.

wrong.text: She is one of those students who always studies hard.
wrong.note: Incorrect: 'who' refers back to 'students', not to 'one', requiring a plural verb.

items.before: He is one of the authors who
This is one of the cars that
She is one of those teachers who
It was one of the events that

rule_groups.name: The Only One of + Plural Noun + Who/That
rule_groups.explain: When 'the only one of' is used, the relative clause refers to 'the only one' (singular), so the verb must be singular.

correct.text: He is the only one of the players who has scored.
correct.note: 'The only one' is the true antecedent, so the relative clause takes a singular verb.

wrong.text: He is the only one of the players who have scored.
wrong.note: Incorrect: 'the only one' is singular, overriding the plural noun that follows.

items.before: She is the only one of my friends who
He was the only one of the candidates who
This is the only one of the buildings that
She is the only one of those nurses who

rule_groups.name: What Clauses as Subjects
rule_groups.explain: When a 'what'-clause is the subject, the verb is usually singular unless the clause clearly denotes multiple things.

correct.note: The 'what'-clause is treated as a singular concept here.

wrong.note: Incorrect: 'what they need' as a unit is singular; the complement does not change this.

rule_groups.name: More than One / Many a
rule_groups.explain: 'More than one' and 'many a' are followed by a singular noun and take a singular verb despite implying plurality.

correct.note: 'More than one' is grammatically singular even though it implies multiple instances.

wrong.note: Incorrect: the expression 'more than one' requires singular agreement.

rule_groups.name: Inverted Word Order (Subject After Verb)
rule_groups.explain: In questions, after negative adverbs (never, rarely, hardly), and in some formal structures, the subject follows the verb but still determines agreement.

correct.note: The subject is 'she' (singular); inversion does not change agreement.

wrong.note: Incorrect: the inverted subject 'she' remains singular.

rule_groups.name: Subjunctive Mood (Wishes, Demands, Suggestions)
rule_groups.explain: In subjunctive clauses after 'demand', 'suggest', 'insist', 'recommend', and in wishes, the verb is the base form regardless of the subject.

correct.note: The subjunctive uses the base form 'study' even with third-person singular 'he'.

wrong.note: Incorrect: in formal subjunctive, the -s is dropped regardless of the subject.

items.before: The judge demanded that the witness
It is recommended that every student
